assessment_summary: The manuscript reports a purposive expert survey (51/92 responses) on 50 prospective AGI safety and governance practices. Main threats arise from sampling and measurement. The sampling frame is author-constructed and leans toward AGI labs; representativeness is unclear, nonresponse may be correlated with views, and subgroup sizes are small, limiting power and potentially inflating "consensus." Items were intentionally abstract, often normatively framed ("should do X"), and treated with an interval Likert mean; these design choices likely increase agreement and complicate interpretation of effect sizes. Twenty items were optional, yielding heterogeneous Ns across items; analyses do not weight or adjust for this or for sector composition. The claim of no item-level differences uses many chi-squared tests with limited power; nulls are not strong evidence of similarity. There is little probing of reasons, feasibility constraints, or tradeoffs behind responses; "I don't know" rates are reported but not modeled. Policy implications sometimes outpace the descriptive nature of the evidence. Open-science practice is strong (pre-registration, code, instrument), yet the embargoed demographic/text microdata reduce reanalysis and robustness checks. Departures from the pre-analysis plan are documented but noteworthy. Overall, this is a clear, timely map of expert views, but generalizability and inferential strength are modest at present.

Study builds a 30 m random-forest model of pantropical natural forest regeneration potential trained on mapped regrowth 2000–2016 and predicts 215 Mha suitable by 2030, with 23.4 Gt C aboveground accumulation over 30 years. Key threats to validity: labels derive from a previous regrowth map with high omission in humid forests and modest user accuracy; presence–absence sampling may embed mapping biases and class imbalance realities are not reflected in balanced training/validation. Spatial autocorrelation is only partially addressed; no strict spatial block cross-validation or calibration of probabilistic outputs is shown, yet probabilities are summed to area (yielding implausibly tight CIs). Predictions use mixed-resolution predictors; several coarser layers (300 m–1 km) drive 30 m outputs, risking artefacts and overinterpretation of fine-scale variation. Natural regeneration “potential” is defined biophysically; socioeconomic feasibility, land tenure, fire risk, reclearance, and policy dynamics are not modeled, so realizable area may be much lower. Carbon estimates downscale 1 km accumulation rates to 30 m and ignore edge effects, disturbances and permanence; belowground C and leakage are only approximated. Uncertainty is not propagated across mapping, model, and carbon layers. Data are shared openly, but code is “available on request,” limiting reproducibility. Documentation is clear but some methods need detail.
